conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Smith. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you came in today because of chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. It started a few days ago—just pressure in the middle of my chest. But last night it got worse, sharp and tight. I woke up at 4 a.m. with it again and some trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you took nitroglycerin then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one tablet. It helped a little, but not completely. I was already coming in for an appointment, so I figured I’d go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good call. Your EKG showed some changes—new T-wave inversions in AVL—which can be concerning. But your troponin levels were normal, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a heart attack?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not based on the blood tests. But given your history—multiple stents, heart disease—we need to be cautious. We’re admitting you to monitor your symptoms and do further testing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve had chest pain before, but this felt different—more intense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why we’re taking it seriously. We’ve started you on heparin to prevent clots, and you’ll have a nuclear stress test soon to check blood flow to your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on Xarelto already. Why heparin too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because we might do a procedure, and we need to temporarily bridge your anticoagulation. We’ve held your Xarelto for now and will restart it after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most are continued. We adjusted your insulin since you’re not eating much. Metformin and linaclotide are held temporarily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also had some mild stomach pain. Nothing severe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noted that. Your exam shows mild epigastric tenderness, but no signs of bleeding. We’ll keep an eye on it. The chest X-ray was clear—no pneumonia or fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. My breathing is better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your oxygen levels are stable. We’ll monitor your heart rhythm and repeat labs overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat troponin was still negative. The stress test is scheduled for today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any idea what it might show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It checks for areas of the heart not getting enough blood. Given your symptoms, we’re looking for ischemia—especially in the LAD artery, which supplies the front of the heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had stents there before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. If there’s a new blockage or restenosis, we’ll see it. If not, it might be small vessel disease or non-cardiac pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The stress test is back. There’s a small, reversible defect in the LAD territory—meaning that area isn’t getting enough blood during stress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it is heart-related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. But it’s a small area, and your ejection fraction is normal—60%. We’ll do a coronary angiogram tomorrow to look directly at your arteries.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another stent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see. If there’s a significant blockage, yes. If not, we may adjust your meds instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re about to take you for the angiogram. It’s a minimally invasive test where we inject dye into your coronary arteries and take X-rays.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any risks?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Low risk. We’ll monitor for bleeding, allergic reaction, or kidney issues. You’re allergic to iohexol, so we’ll use a different contrast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The angiogram is done. Good news—your stents are open, and there’s no significant restenosis. The disease is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why the chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s due to small vessel disease in the diagonal branches of the LAD—tiny arteries that don’t show up on angiogram. The stress test picked it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not a blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not a major one. But the small vessels can still cause ischemia. We’re increasing your Imdur from 30mg to 60mg daily to help prevent angina.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that stop the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should reduce frequency and severity. We’re also keeping you on clopidogrel and restarting Xarelto. Aspirin is being held due to bleeding risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure? I’ve been feeling a bit lightheaded.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pressures have been on the lower side—around 100/60 at times. That’s why we held your losartan. You can restart it once your outpatient doctor checks your BP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my diabetes meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Back to your usual—metformin and insulin. We adjusted doses while you were NPO, but now you’re back on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the stomach pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still mild. We switched you to omeprazole briefly, but you’re back on esomeprazole. If it persists, your doctor may consider further GI workup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re being discharged today. Your symptoms have resolved, and all tests are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your meds as prescribed—especially the new 60mg Imdur. Watch your blood pressure before restarting losartan. Use nitroglycerin if chest pain returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any activity restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No heavy lifting for a few days. Walk as tolerated. Follow up with cardiology in one week and your primary doctor for BP check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the chest pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take nitroglycerin. If it doesn’t help after three doses, or if you have shortness of breath, go to the ER immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll send all instructions to your doctors. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—we’re sending you home with an opioid for pain, but please discuss long-term use with your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s just for breakthrough pain. I’ll talk to my provider.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Nurse will go over your discharge papers now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Smith. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.
